scenario: Today's AI search track is about better retrieval not automatically giving better answers. One study decides per question whether to add a hybrid retrieval pass, keeping the evidence hit rate while skipping most extra calls, yet answers do not get more reliable. SpectRAG uses a chunk graph to fill in multi-hop evidence, with large recall gains but small answer gains. Two more papers tackle cost and risk: a government service assistant routes most requests to fixed templates and checks every amount, and MetaKV reuses recurring structures in GraphRAG to save prefill.

papers.title: When Is Additional Retrieval Worthwhile? A Cost-Aware Study of Evidence Gain and Answer Reliability in RAG
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can benefit from more sophisticated retrieval, but extra retrieval may be unnecessary for many questions and gains in evidence retrieval may not translate into faithful or correct answers. We study a cost-aware, two-action retrieval policy that chooses between a dense-retrieval-plus-reranking baseline and a hybrid lexical--dense retriever. Rather than classifying baseline retrieval as simply successful or unsuccessful, we estimate the question-specific incremental evidence-retrieval benefit of hybrid retrieval using features available before the routing decision. A regularized linear model and decision threshold are selected using document-grouped cross-validation and frozen prior to held-out evaluation. On 60 previously unseen QASPER training-split articles (188 questions, 169 evidence-evaluable), the policy triggers hybrid retrieval on 46 questions (24.5\%) and obtains the same evidence Hit@10 as always-hybrid retrieval (78.70\%, versus 76.92\% for always-keep). Paired, paper-cluster bootstrap intervals do not establish a reliable utility advantage. We further compare generated answers from a 4-bit Qwen3-4B model under the three retrieval policies. Provisional answer-level assessments show no clear correctness or faithfulness improvement after partial review, despite the evidence-retrieval result. The generation assessments remain model-assisted and lack independent human validation. These results expose an important distinction between retrieving relevant evidence efficiently and improving the reliability of the generated answer. The work is presented as a reproducible empirical study, not a claim of statistically established answer-quality superiority.
papers.summary: Is adding a second retrieval pass to RAG worth it? This paper first gets evidence with vector retrieval plus reranking, then has a small linear model read the scores left by that pass, such as how high the top-1 similarity is and how far it sits above the second result. From those it predicts whether switching to hybrid BM25-plus-vector retrieval would find more evidence, and it switches only when the predicted gain is large enough. On papers from QASPER (a QA dataset over research papers) that were never used in training, it switched only 24.5% of questions to hybrid retrieval and matched the evidence hit rate of always using hybrid retrieval, 78.70% for both. Yet when a small model generated answers from that evidence, neither correctness nor faithfulness improved. ==Finding evidence more cheaply does not make answers more reliable==, and gains in retrieval metrics cannot be read as gains in answer quality.

papers.title: Governed Sovereign RAG for Public Administration: Tripartite Epistemic Routing, Facet-Guided Clarification, and Deterministic Numeric Verification in Citizen Services
papers.abstract: Deploying conversational assistants at government service desks faces a tension between regulatory certainty (zero tolerance for invented fees), data sovereignty prohibiting commercial clouds, and high rates of underspecified or out-of-jurisdiction citizen queries. We present and evaluate a governed, sovereign Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture deployed on the official portal of the State of Tlaxcala, Mexico (tlaxcaladigital.gob.mx), covering 1,143 procedures and a decoupled directory of 924 offices. The system governs interactions via three pillars: (1) a two-stage tripartite epistemic gate (clarify_policy and a Boltzmann distribution over AnyJev) arbitrating among answering (SPECIFIC), facet-guided clarification (CLARIFY), and abstaining (ABSTAIN); (2) a post-generation deterministic numeric verifier (verify_numeric_guardrail) with SHA-256 cache invalidation ensuring every generated fee or validity figure belongs to the retrieved official record; and (3) an empirical evaluation across 380 organic production traces (8 weeks) and a 200-query stratified benchmark (5-fold CV: 86.41% +/- 7.50%). In production, 89.47% of traffic is resolved at Level 0 via deterministic templates without free generation (global p50 = 0.665 s; direct L0 p50 = 0.445 s; slow-tail p95 = 30.412 s under CPU queuing), with 0/40 fiscal amount hallucinations observed in Level 1 (95% bound <= 8.81%). On the benchmark, the system achieves 86.50% strict Top-1 accuracy (+10.00 pp over a binary neural gate, p = 0.00453, p_Holm = 0.01172), pairing a 93.00% conditional safe upper bound with a 70.87% dropout-adjusted effective resolution after accounting for 53.33% citizen drop-off in clarification menus.
papers.summary: For a government service-desk assistant, one invented fee is an incident, and citizens' questions are often vague or outside the agency's jurisdiction. The official portal of the Mexican state of Tlaxcala runs a RAG assistant on local servers. For each question it first decides whether to answer, to ask for the missing detail, or to refuse because the matter is outside the state's jurisdiction. After generating an answer, a program checks every fee and validity period against the retrieved official record. Across 380 real conversations after launch, 89.47% were answered with fixed templates, with no free generation at all; no invented amounts appeared in the audited generated answers. ==Where zero errors are tolerated, routing most requests away from free generation and adding a deterministic check to the rest== is more robust than simply improving generation quality.

papers.title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.
papers.authors: Zafer Sahinoglu, Abdulazeez Mohammed, Buse Yaren Kazangirler, Cahit Berkay Kazangirler
papers.summary: In multi-hop QA, retrieval recall jumps a lot while answers improve only a little. Offline, SpectRAG links document chunks into a graph: two chunks get an edge if they are semantically close, adjacent in the source, mention the same entities or cite each other, and these signals are weighted into the edge weight. At query time, vector retrieval and BM25 first hit some chunks, which then pass their relevance scores to neighbors along the edges, more to closer neighbors, so chunks that look unlike the question but are intermediate reasoning steps can be recovered. Finally it picks a low-redundancy context within about 12k tokens. On MultiHopRAG, its recall over the top 5 results is 64.7 versus 49.2 for the graph-retrieval baseline LightRAG. Yet its answer EM is only 1.5 points higher than LightRAG's. ==A large recall lead shrinks to a small edge at generation time==, so multi-hop RAG should be judged on both retrieval and answers.

papers.title: Structure Is All You Need to Reuse: Accelerating GraphRAG via Meta-Structure-Aware KV Caching
papers.authors: Ruikun Luo, Changwei Gu, Jing Yang, Hongming Liang, Yuan Gao
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Knowledge Graphs (GraphRAG) enhances Large Language Models (LLMs) with structured, multi-hop evidence. However, existing GraphRAG systems predominantly linearize retrieved subgraphs into long textual prompts, forcing LLMs to recompute identical schema-level reasoning across queries repeatedly. This text-centric design incurs substantial prefilling latency, memory overhead, and severely limited cache reuse under entity-level variations. We observe that although retrieved entities differ across queries, their underlying logical schemas (meta-structures) recur with high frequency, indicating that most computational cost is spent on repeatedly encoding invariant structural logic. In this paper, we propose MetaKV, the first structure-aware KV caching mechanism that explicitly decouples static structural logic from dynamic entity semantics in GraphRAG inference. In a preparation phase, MetaKV mines frequent meta-structures and pre-computes their Key-Value

papers.summary: Every time GraphRAG answers a question, it flattens the retrieved subgraph into a long text and makes the LLM redo prefill. Yet while different questions retrieve different entities, the relational structure among them recurs again and again, so most compute goes into re-encoding the same structure. MetaKV mines these frequent structures in advance, turns each into a skeleton with empty slots, and precomputes the skeleton's KV cache. At inference it fetches the matching skeleton's cache, computes fresh representations only for this question's entities, and places them in the skeleton's reserved slots to assemble the full context. On HotpotQA and MetaQA, prefill is up to 6.4 times faster with a 73% effective cache-hit rate, while reasoning accuracy stays competitive. ==Entities change but the structure does not, so the structure should not be recomputed every time==.
